summary:
Belize decriminalised same-sex conduct through the courts. On 10 August 2016 the Supreme Court, presided over by Chief Justice Kenneth Benjamin, struck down the colonial-era Section 53 sodomy law as unconstitutional in the challenge LGBT advocate Caleb Orozco filed in 2010 and which was heard in Belize City in May 2013. On 30 December 2019 the Appeals Court upheld that finding of unconstitutionality and confirmed that the Constitution's protections against discrimination extend to sexual orientation and that freedom of expression encompasses sexual expression. Belize was the first former British Caribbean territory to overturn such a statute.

Entry rules remain a separate matter. Section 5(1)(e) of Belize's Immigration Act lists "any prostitute or homosexual" among prohibited immigrants. Jamaican activist Maurice Tomlinson filed a challenge in 2013, obtained leave from the Caribbean Court of Justice in May 2014, and was joined by CARICOM as an interested party in October 2014; on 10 June 2016 the Caribbean Court of Justice dismissed his case, finding no violation of his freedom of movement. Belize contended during that litigation that Section 5(1) reaches only persons offering sexual services for financial gain and is not applied as a blanket bar on homosexual immigrants. The 10 June 2016 judgment further clarified that neither Belize nor Trinidad and Tobago may exclude homosexuals from other CARICOM states given their obligations under the Treaty of Chaguaramas, notwithstanding domestic statutes that appear to ban entry by gay people.

Statutory protections now sit alongside that case law. The Anti-Sexual Harassment Act 2024 expressly covers prevention and protection from sexual harassment irrespective of sexual preference and gender identity. Section 8(1)(c)(i) of the Alternative Sentencing Act 2024 makes evidence that an offence was motivated by bias, prejudice or hate based on sexual orientation an aggravating circumstance in sentencing, effective 27 April 2024.

Official machinery shows both cooperation and resistance. In its 2018 Universal Periodic Review Belize accepted 15 of 17 sexual-orientation and gender-identity recommendations, the first CARICOM state to accept that many, pledging legal reform, explicit anti-discrimination legislation, police training and SOGI data collection while noting rather than accepting two rights-equality recommendations. The same review accepted recommendations on educational campaigns against societal stigma, universal access to HIV treatment for LGBT people, action on discrimination, violence and hate crimes, and training police officials to respond properly to violence; those recommendations came largely from Argentina, Australia, Brazil, Chile, France, Germany, Iceland, Ireland, Italy, Mexico, Spain, Ukraine, the United States and Uruguay.

The government's own conduct after the 2016 ruling ran the other way. It announced on 17 August 2016 that it would not appeal, then reversed course after meeting religious leaders on 9 September and filed a partial appeal against the declaration that the Constitution bars discrimination based on sexual orientation; the Catholic Church withdrew from that appeal in March 2018, leaving the government as sole appellant. Solicitor General Nigel Hawke argued the ruling was judicial overreach in reading "sex" to include sexual orientation. Religious bodies campaigned openly against decriminalisation: the Council of Churches held a "Take a Stand" rally on 3 December 2011 and a "Belize Action/Family Forum" rally on 23 November 2011 that described the change as "an orchestrated plan of demonic darkness", and in December 2011 Prime Minister Dean Barrow publicly rejected pressure from President Obama, stating that Belize would not alter its laws.

Violence risk has been concrete rather than theoretical. The Supreme Court case was heard in May 2013 amid violence and death threats directed at LGBT activists. Before the ruling the statute was rarely enforced, yet expat reporting holds that it had fostered intolerance, citing a 1998 protest against a gay cruise docking as evidence of residual public hostility; the same reporting states that gay travellers have long found Belize friendly. A 2013 UNAIDS survey of 773 Belizeans aged 18 to 64 found 34% accepting and 34% tolerant of homosexuals, among the highest acceptance rates recorded in Caribbean polling.

Visibility has increased since the ruling. Belize held its first Pride Week in August 2017 with awareness and acceptance activities hosted throughout the country, and LGBT organisations including UNIBAM have become more visible and active since August 2016. The Human Dignity Trust carries the case among its documentation of constitutional challenges to anti-sodomy statutes.
tangentialFactors:
Belize is a point of comparison in regional pattern-setting rather than an outlier. The Human Dignity Trust groups Belize with constitutional challenges to anti-sodomy statutes across the Eastern Caribbean, and the 2016 decision made Belize the first former British Caribbean colony to overturn such a law, a sequence other post-colonial jurisdictions in the region have since followed or resisted.

The 2018 Universal Periodic Review count is likewise comparative: 15 of 17 SOGI recommendations accepted made Belize the first CARICOM country to accept that proportion, and the 2013 UNAIDS acceptance figures place Belize among the more tolerant societies polled in the Caribbean even though that same polling leaves a third of the population neither accepting nor tolerant.

Turbulence in the record is driven by organised religious opposition rather than street crime statistics. Rallies in November and December 2011, the government's reversal on appeal within a month of the 2016 judgment, and the Solicitor General's overreach argument all indicate that decriminalisation remains contested at institutional level, and death threats against activists in 2013 show the contest has previously turned violent.
localsOnly:
Residents gain an express statutory shield against sexual harassment on grounds of sexual preference and gender identity under the Anti-Sexual Harassment Act 2024, and a bias motive based on sexual orientation now aggravates sentencing under the Alternative Sentencing Act 2024 from 27 April 2024.

Residents also benefit from the 30 December 2019 Appeals Court confirmation that constitutional non-discrimination protections cover sexual orientation and that freedom of expression includes sexual expression, a holding with bearing on public advocacy, media and association.

The government has pledged legal reform, explicit anti-discrimination legislation, police training and the collection of sexual-orientation and gender-identity data, and has accepted recommendations on anti-stigma educational campaigns, universal HIV treatment access for LGBT people, action against discrimination, violence and hate crimes, and police training for responding to violence. Whether that pledged anti-discrimination legislation has been enacted is not stated in the available sources.

Organised community life is established: UNIBAM operates as an advocacy organisation, the country held its first Pride Week in August 2017 with activities hosted nationwide, and LGBT organisations have been more visible and active since the August 2016 ruling.

Residents who are immigrants face the Immigration Act provision listing homosexuals among prohibited persons, which the Belize government argued applies only to sexual services offered for financial gain; the Caribbean Court of Justice judgment constrains exclusion under the regional treaty framework.
outOfScopeNotes:
Prisoner placement for transgender detainees is unresolved. A general survey of LGBTQ people in prison was retrieved successfully but contains no Belize-specific practice: no rule on housing by birth sex versus gender identity, no dedicated units, and no documented solitary or segregation practice for trans prisoners in Belize. There is no usable finding on this question.

No youth- or minor-specific findings on care, medication or travel appear in the available sources, and none should be inferred from the general adult material above.

Whether the Immigration Act provision naming homosexuals has been applied to an actual traveller since the 2016 Caribbean Court of Justice judgment, and how border officers now exercise that discretion, is not sourced.

Whether the police training, SOGI data collection and anti-discrimination legislation pledged at the 2018 Universal Periodic Review have been implemented is not sourced; the recommendations are documented as accepted, not as delivered.

The 1998 protest and the 2011 rallies are attested in secondary reporting and do not establish current levels of hostility; recent hate-crime incidence against LGBT people in Belize is not quantified in the inventory.
